title: Three turnings
hook: a Mahayana map of three turnings of the wheel; other schools map it differently

segments.voice: Yesterday, what all share: precepts, a trained mind and kindness under every robe. Your line was the common ground. Did your one precept ask anything of you? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

In a deer park near Benares, the Buddha gives his first teaching to a few old companions who had once walked away from him. The four truths. The middle way. The Pali text says that when he finished, the cry went up from the earth to the heavens: the wheel of the teaching has been set rolling. A wheel set rolling. It's a strong picture, and the schools took it in different directions. Some say that wheel turned once, at the deer park, and has been rolling ever since. Others say it turned again, and then a third time. Today, the map of three turnings, and why the maps differ.
screen: `THE DEER PARK.` → `THE WHEEL SET ROLLING.` → `ONCE, OR THREE TIMES?`

segments.voice: First, the deer park itself. In the Pali canon this talk is the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, setting the wheel of dhamma in motion. Rhys Davids gave it a grand English title: The Foundation of the Kingdom of Righteousness. Every map in today's lesson starts from this talk. Second, the Mahayana map. A Mahayana scripture, the Samdhinirmocana Sutra, describes the teaching as turning in three stages. The first turning: the four truths, taught at the deer park. The second: the teaching of emptiness, found in the Perfection of Wisdom sutras. The third: a turning that explains and clarifies the second, carefully distinguishing what is meant literally from what needs interpreting. That map became important in Tibet. Third, the maps inside the map. Tibetan schools don't agree on which turning is final. Some hold that the second, on emptiness, is the definitive word. Others give that place to the third. Each school sets out its reasons in long, careful debate. In China, Tiantai teachers drew a different map again, arranging the sutras into periods of the Buddha's teaching life. Fourth, the Theravada view. The Theravada keeps the Pali canon as the Buddha's word and doesn't accept the later sutras into it. For a Theravada teacher, the wheel set rolling at the deer park is the wheel, still turning, and there is no second or third. Every one of these maps is a way of ordering a huge body of teaching. A map shows how its maker walks the land. Each school explains its own, and they can be laid side by side without one being torn up.
screen: `THE WHEEL SET ROLLING AT THE DEER PARK.` · `A MAHAYANA MAP: THREE TURNINGS.` · `TIBETAN SCHOOLS WEIGH THEM DIFFERENTLY.` · `THERAVADA: ONE WHEEL, STILL TURNING.` · then, large: `MAPS DIFFER.`

segments.voice: Here's something to try, with a pencil or just in your mind. Draw the deer park as a small circle. From it, draw one long line, the Theravada wheel rolling on. Then, beside it, draw three rings, the Mahayana turnings. Don't put either one on top. Lay them side by side, the way you'd lay two maps of the same coastline on a table. Now sit with your breath, and look at both. Notice any urge to pick a winner, and let it rest. The bell holds the time.
Three turnings. A Mahayana map of the teaching in three stages: the four truths, emptiness, and a clarifying turning. Other schools draw the map differently. Today's word.
Your line: maps differ. Today, when someone describes something you know in a way you wouldn't, ask what their map is for before you correct it. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Tibetan monastic colleges study the three turnings in depth and debate which is definitive, while Theravada teachers keep the Pali canon and its first discourse at the deer park as the turning of the wheel.

pairs: the four truths, at the deer park

fork.setup: a Tibetan teacher shows you the three turnings. that afternoon a Theravada monk tells you the wheel turned once. what do you do?
options: work out which of them is right before going further.
lay both maps side by side: each orders the teaching its own way.
fork.reveal: the schools themselves do this: each explains its own map, and even the Tibetan schools weigh the turnings differently.

original.note: Sanskrit dharmacakra (Pali dhammacakka): the wheel of the teaching.

trapdoor: what you thought: three turnings means the Buddha gave three talks.
what it means: a Mahayana way of ordering the whole teaching into three stages: the truths, emptiness, and clarification.
what a scholar hears: the Samdhinirmocana Sutra's scheme, read differently across Tibetan schools, and not used in the Theravada.

notes: The three turnings are attributed to the Samdhinirmocana Sutra (chapter 7 in common divisions); confirm the chapter and the description of the third turning as distinguishing literal from interpretable meaning.
Tibetan schools: some (e.g., Gelug) hold the second turning definitive, others (e.g., Jonang, and some readings in other schools) the third. Script names no school; confirm the general claim is fair.
Tiantai 'arranging the sutras into periods of the Buddha's teaching life': confirm; the traditional number of periods was left out on purpose.
Theravada does not accept Mahayana sutras into the canon: confirm wording is fair and not dismissive.
Hook: 'a few old companions who had once walked away from him' and the cry rising from earth to heavens are paraphrased from SN 56.11 and the Vinaya; confirm.
